author: Basil of Caesarea
occasion: Basil preaches on the day of the resurrection commemoration, when members of his flock, especially women, formed choruses at the martyrs' shrines before the city and turned the holy day into drunken dancing and lewd behavior.
argument: Basil laments that one evening and one assault of the enemy have undone all his Lenten exhortations. He describes drunkenness as a voluntary demon that destroys reason, makes people worse than animals, and ruins both soul and body. He rebukes the general behavior of drunkards, including their elaborate drinking parties and sexual shamelessness, warning that such behavior excludes people from God's kingdom. He closes by urging repentance through fasting, psalmody, tears, almsgiving, and separation from the unrepentant.

outline.move: Basil opens by lamenting that one evening and one assault of the enemy have undone all his Lenten exhortations, and he describes the scandalous behavior of women at the martyrs' shrines before the city.
He defines drunkenness as a voluntary demon and shows how it destroys reason, making drunkards worse than animals.
He describes the varied passions produced by wine, including despair, rage, and unnatural lust, and compares drunkards to storm-tossed ships.
He explains how constant drinking dulls the senses, and he applies the prophet's 'woe' to drunkards, detailing the physical damage wine causes.
He invokes Isaiah's woe against those who pursue drink from early morning, and he describes the elaborate drinking parties of drunkards with their officials, contests, and prizes.

He laments the ruin of young men, compares drunkards to idols, and describes the drinking practices of drunkards, including a device for equal drinking, before turning to the lewd songs and dances of both sexes.

He warns that even those who escaped bodily sin were corrupted in soul, threatens judgment, and prescribes repentance through fasting, psalmody, tears, almsgiving, and separation from the unrepentant.

_unresolved_facts.claim: members of his flock, especially women, formed choruses at the martyrs' shrines before the city and turned the holy day into drunken dancing and lewd behavior
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Γυναῖκες ἀκόλαστοι, ἐπιλαθόμεναι τοῦ φόβου τοῦ Θεοῦ... ἐν τοῖς πρὸ τῆς πόλεως μαρτυ ρίοις χοροὺς συστησάμεναι, ἐργαστήριον τῆς οἰκείας αὐτῶν ἀσχημοσύνης τοὺς ἡγιασμένους τόπους πεποίηνται
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief should specify that Basil explicitly names only women in this initial scandal—'licentious women' (γυναῖκες ἀκόλαστοι) who formed choruses at the martyrs' shrines. Men are not mentioned in section 1; the general behavior of drunkards and mixed-sex carousing appears only in later sections (6-7).

_unresolved_facts.claim: the day of the resurrection commemoration
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τοιαύτῃ, ὅτε αὐτὰς ἐχρῆν διὰ τὴν ἀνάμνησιν τῆς ἀναστάσεως καθῆσθαι ἐν τοῖς οἵ κοις
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says 'on such a day, when they ought to have sat at home because of the commemoration of the resurrection'—this refers to the resurrection commemoration as the expected context for proper behavior, but does not explicitly state this IS the day of resurrection (Pascha). The mention of 'the seven weeks of the fast' (τῶν ἑπτὰ τούτων τῆς νηστείας ἑβδομάδων) and later 'How will Pentecost receive you, thus having insulted Pascha?' (Πῶς ὑμᾶς ἡ Πεντηκοστὴ ὑποδέξεται, οὕτω τοῦ Πάσχα καθυβρισθέντος;) in section 7 suggests the homily was delivered during the Paschal season, likely near or after Pascha itself, with the scandal having occurred during that period.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He describes drunkenness as a voluntary demon that destroys reason, makes people worse than animals, and ruins both soul and body
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Μέθη, ὁ αὐθαίρετος δαίμων, ἐξ ἡδονῆς ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἐμβαλλόμενος
_unresolved_facts.fix: Basil calls drunkenness 'a self-chosen demon' (αὐθαίρετος δαίμων), not merely 'voluntary'—the Greek emphasizes that the drunkard actively chooses this demon, not that the demon itself is voluntary. The nuance of αὐθαίρετος ('self-chosen, of one's own accord') is stronger than 'voluntary' suggests.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections: ['2'], move: 'He defines drunkenness as a voluntary demon and shows how it destroys reason, making drunkards worse than animals'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ τῶν βοσκημά των φαίην ἂν ἔγωγε ἀλογωτέρους εἶναι τοὺς ἐν τῇ μέθῃ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The comparison to animals appears in section 2, but the claim that drunkards are 'worse than animals' is incomplete. Basil specifically says they are 'more irrational than cattle' (ἀλογωτέρους) because animals have fixed mating seasons while drunkards pursue unnatural lusts 'at every time and hour' (πάντα καιρὸν καὶ πᾶσαν ὥραν). The unnatural/unnatural lust aspect is central and omitted.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections: ['3'], move: 'He describes the varied passions produced by wine, including despair, rage, and unnatural lust, and compares drunkards to storm-tossed ships'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἕτεροι δὲ εἰς τὰ ἐναντία περιάγονται πάθη. Δυσέλπιδές εἰσι, καὶ κατηφεῖς, καὶ ὀδυνηροί, καὶ δακρυώδεις, καὶ ψοφοδεεῖς, καὶ εὐπτόητοι
_unresolved_facts.fix: The outline mentions 'despair, rage, and unnatural lust' but the source lists: hopeless, downcast, painful, tearful, noise-fearing, easily frightened (δυσέλπιδές, κατηφεῖς, ὀδυνηροί, δακρυώδεις, ψοφοδεεῖς, εὐπτόητοι). 'Rage' is not in this list; the 'opposite passions' are depressive/anxious states, not rage. The 'unnatural lust' appears later in section 3 but is not part of this initial catalogue of opposite passions.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections: ['6'], move: 'He laments the ruin of young men, compares drunkards to idols, and describes the drinking practices of drunkards, including a device for equal drinking, before turning to the lewd songs and dances of both sexes'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τί γὰρ ἄλλο εἰσὶν οἱ μεθύοντες ἢ τὰ εἴδωλα τῶν ἐθνῶν; Ὀφθαλμοὺς ἔχουσι, καὶ οὐ βλέπουσιν...
_unresolved_facts.fix: The 'idols' comparison is accurate, but the outline misses that Basil specifically addresses a host directly: 'Ἄνθρωπε, παρά ταξιν ἐποίησας τὸ συμπόσιον' ('Man, you have made the symposium out of order'). This second-person rebuke to the host who enables drinking is a significant structural element that the brief's 'voices' section partially captures but the outline omits.

_unresolved_facts.claim: speaker: 'Basil (addressing a drinker directly)', how_marked: 'second-person singular rebuke to the drunkard', sections: ['5']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τίνι οὐαί; τίνι θόρυβος; τίνι κρίσεις; τίνι ἀηδίαι καὶ λέσχαι; τίνι συντρίμματα διακενῆς; τίνος πελιδνοὶ οἱ ὀφθαλμοί; Οὐ τῶν ἐγχρονιζόντων ἐν οἴνῳ...
_unresolved_facts.fix: The second-person singular in section 5 is actually a series of rhetorical questions with third-person identification ('whose eyes are livid? Is it not those who linger in wine?'), not direct address to a drinker. The direct second-person singular rebuke to a drinker appears in section 6: 'Κατάκυψόν σου πρὸς τὴν ἀθλίαν γαστέρα' ('Bend down to your wretched stomach'). The voices entry should be corrected to section 6 or recharacterized.

_unresolved_facts.claim: speaker: 'Basil (addressing a host directly)', how_marked: 'second-person singular rebuke to the host who enables drinking', sections: ['6']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἄνθρωπε, παρά ταξιν ἐποίησας τὸ συμπόσιον. Ἐκβάλλεις τοὺς νεανίσκους χειραγωγουμένους... καὶ καλεῖς μὲν ὡς φίλον ἐπὶ τὸ δεῖπνον, ἐκβάλλεις δὲ νεκρόν, οἴνῳ τὴν ζωὴν αὐτοῦ κατασβέσας
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief correctly identifies the host address in section 6, but 'how_marked' should note the specific vocative 'Ἄνθρωπε' ('Man/O man') and the dramatic structure: the host calls a friend to dinner but casts out a corpse, having extinguished his life with wine.

_unresolved_facts.claim: name: 'Jeremiah', source_forms: ['Ἱερεμίου'], who: 'prophet cited as an example of compelled speech'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: εἰ μὴ ἐφοβούμην τὸ ὑπόδειγμα τοῦ Ἱερεμίου, ὃς, πρὸς ἀπειθῆ λαὸν φθέγγεσθαι μὴ βουλόμενος, ἔπαθεν ἐκεῖνα ἅπερ αὐτὸς διηγήσατο
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source form is Ἱερεμίου (genitive), but the nominative would be Ἱερεμίας. More importantly, Jeremiah is not merely 'cited as an example of compelled speech'—Basil fears becoming like Jeremiah, who suffered burning fire within when he tried to remain silent before a disobedient people. The 'who' description understates the parallel: Basil presents himself as potentially in Jeremiah's position, compelled to speak despite the futility.

_unresolved_facts.claim: name: 'Cain', source_forms: ['Κάϊν'], who: 'biblical figure whose curse of trembling Basil applies to drunkards'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τί τὴν κατάραν τοῦ Κάϊν ἐφ' ἑαυ τὸν ἐπισπᾶσαι, τρέμων καὶ περιφερόμενος διὰ παντὸς τοῦ βίου;
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source form is actually Κάϊν (nominative), not genitive. More substantively, Basil asks 'Why do you draw the curse of Cain upon yourself?'—the drunkard is actively bringing this curse upon himself, not merely having it applied to him. The 'who' description should capture this self-inflicted aspect.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He refers to Isaiah and Jeremiah by name and quotes the Gospels
_unresolved_facts.fix: No Gospel quotation is identifiable in the source text. Basil quotes or alludes to: Jeremiah (by name), Isaiah (by name), Proverbs or wisdom tradition ('strong shall be strongly tested' / 'δυνατοὶ δὲ δυνατῶς ἐτασθήσονται'), 1 Corinthians 6:10 ('drunkards will not inherit the kingdom of God' / 'Μέθυσοι βασιλείαν Θεοῦ οὐ κληρονομήσουσι'), Ephesians 5:18 ('do not get drunk with wine' / 'Μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ, ἐν ᾧ ἐστιν ἀσωτία'), Sirach/Ecclesiasticus ('wine is unruly, and drunkenness is insolent' / 'Ἀκόλαστον οἶνος, καὶ ὑβριστικὸν μέθη'), and Exodus 32 (the Levites). The Gospels are not directly quoted.
